catalog_quote: O acento é uma propriedade prosódica culminativa da palavra. Logo, em uma palavra prosódica, somente uma sílaba pode ser a mais forte ... Em Dâw, é o tom que exerce a função lexical e o acento, por sua vez, possui a função de demarcar a palavra prosódica e sua atribuição é previsível por regras. ... O acento em Dâw é fixo e incide na última sílaba da palavra. Há uma correlação entre ocorrência do acento e do tom em palavras simples e compostas. Nestas palavras, há um só tom contrastivo, atribuído à sílaba tônica. Em palavras atonais, a manifestação do acento na última sílaba da palavra faz com que ela seja percebida como tendo um tom fixo mais alto que a sílaba átona precedente. ... new_statements.quote: Where lexemes have more than one syllable, primary stress falls on the final syllable. [ms p. 3] ... Stress in Dâw is consistently word-final. Unstressed syllables bear a default low tone, as in the first syllable of /tʃokwét/ [tʃ'òkˈwét] 'toucan'. Word-final syllables lacking a consonantal coda consistently have falling tone (and a long vowel), as in /tûː/ 'ground'. Note that words in Dâw have exactly one H pitch, always occurring on the stressed syllable. We analyze this as a constraint that a lexeme have one obligatory and cumulative H tone that must dock onto the stressed syllable. Any tone-bearing unit not linked to this H tone receives a L tone by default. [ms p. 5-6]
new_statements.citation: Simmons, Mark & Patience Epps. 2025. Tonogenesis in the Naduhup family of northwest Amazonia. Diachronica 42(3-4): 479-507.
new_statements.locator: HAL author manuscript (halshs-05224808v1), §2 'The Naduhup languages' ms p. 3 (PDF p. 5) and §3.1 'Dâw: tone and vowel length' ms p. 5 (PDF p. 7); journal pagination 479-507 not available in this copy
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (fixed final). Refines it with the tonal side: one obligatory, cumulative H docked on the stressed final syllable; length and tone contrasts restricted to that syllable; the system is described as a 'word-accent' system parasitic on lexical stress. The authors also note (ms p. 5-6) that their stress-based analysis differs from that of S. Martins (2004) and V. Martins (2005), who treat the contours as underlying tone with H as a phonetic effect of stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is always on the final syllable of the word (family-wide: primary stress on the final syllable of any polysyllabic lexeme). Dâw is at the same time a 'word-accent' tone language: every word carries exactly one H pitch, which sits on the stressed (final) syllable; unstressed syllables get default L. Tone (H on short vowels; rising vs falling on long vowels) and vowel length contrast only in that stressed syllable. Ms p. 4: 'only one long vowel and/or contrastive tone is realized per morpheme (and, in most cases, also per phonological word), and always coincides with stress.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Dâw (secondary stress is mentioned only for Swedish/Norwegian in the typological discussion, ms p. 4).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Dâw. For the sister languages the authors specify 'stem-final (word-final when no bound morphology is present)' (ms p. 7, on Hup and Yuhup, introduced with 'As in Dâw'), which suggests the stress domain is the stem when bound morphology is present. Word-final open syllables always have falling tone and a long vowel.
new_statements.identity_note: Neither opened work distinguishes Dâw varieties; both describe the language as a whole (Martins 1994 from his own fieldwork data, Simmons & Epps 2025 from S. Martins 2004 / V. Martins 2005 and their own data). Simmons & Epps's family-level statement (final stress in all four Naduhup languages) is also explicitly applied to Dâw.

new_statements.quote: No cruzamento dos dados apresentados, com a classificação tipológica, Dâw é uma língua pitch-accent (tonal periférica) e não é do tipo tonal verdadeiro, pelo fato de restringir o uso do tom: [...] 2. Palavras dissilábicas do tipo CV(C).CVC têm tom alto na última sílaba [á] e baixo na primeira [à] (cf. 4.3.1.). [p. 123] ... Dâw é uma língua pitch-accent, isto quer dizer que o acento em Dâw se faz pelo pitch. [p. 125] ... Deduz-se desta regra que o tom alto funciona como o acento. 5.3.1 Acento-entonação. O acento que é conhecido como "stress", e/ou loudness, é produzido pelo impulso pulmonar e manifesta-se em Dâw no nível da oração. [...] em Dâw o pitch funciona no nível da palavra e o stress no nível da oração. [p. 126]
new_statements.translation: Crossing the data presented with the typological classification, Dâw is a pitch-accent (peripheral tonal) language and not a true tone language, because it restricts the use of tone: [...] 2. Disyllabic words of the type CV(C).CVC have high tone on the last syllable [á] and low on the first [à] (cf. 4.3.1). [p. 123] ... Dâw is a pitch-accent language, which means that the accent in Dâw is realised by pitch. [p. 125] ... It follows from this rule that the high tone functions as the accent. 5.3.1 Accent-intonation. The accent known as 'stress' and/or loudness is produced by the pulmonary impulse and in Dâw manifests itself at the level of the clause. [...] in Dâw pitch operates at the word level and stress at the clause level. [p. 126]
new_statements.citation: Martins, Valteir. 1994. Análise prosódica da língua Dâw (Makú-Kamã) numa perspectiva não-linear. MA thesis, Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina, Florianópolis. 233 pp.
new_statements.locator: §4.6.7 'Tipologia tonal' p. 123 (PDF p. 134); Chapter 5 'Acento' pp. 124-138, esp. §5.3 'Sistema acentual Dâw' pp. 125-126 (PDF pp. 136-137), §5.3.1 'Acento-entonação' p. 126, §5.3.2 p. 133; conclusion p. 138 (PDF p. 149). Printed page number is at the top of each scanned page; PDF page = printed page + 11.
new_statements.relation_note: Type, not placement, differs. The catalog records fixed final word STRESS; Martins denies word-level stress altogether (stress/loudness is a clause-level intonational phenomenon) and instead posits word-level pitch accent, one H per word. His placement of that H (last syllable in disyllables, p. 123; H on monosyllables) is compatible with the catalog's final position, so the disagreement is about the category (pitch accent vs stress-accent), which Simmons & Epps 2025 explicitly reject in favour of stress with a parasitic H.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Martins analyses Dâw as a pitch accent language: the word carries one high tone, which in CVC monosyllables is level H and in CV(C).CVC disyllables falls on the last syllable (L on the first); the high tone 'functions as the accent'. Intensity stress (loudness) is not a word-level property for him: it operates only at clause level, rising from the first to the last word of an independent clause and falling across a dependent clause (§5.3.2-5.3.3, pp. 133-135; conclusion p. 138: 'O acento (intensidade).. funciona no nível da oração'). He also claims pitch and stress are independent of each other (p. 132).
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal, not stress-related: CV: monosyllables have contour tones; CVVC words with voiceless coda always have low-high (rising) tone, with voiced coda high-low in 70% and low-high in 30% of cases (pp. 123-124, 138); a high-tone noun suffix is said to be dismantling the coda-conditioned system (p. 138-139).
new_statements.identity_note: Neither opened work distinguishes Dâw varieties; both describe the language as a whole (Martins 1994 from his own fieldwork data, Simmons & Epps 2025 from S. Martins 2004 / V. Martins 2005 and their own data). Simmons & Epps's family-level statement (final stress in all four Naduhup languages) is also explicitly applied to Dâw.

readall_conflicts: One analytical disagreement, not a placement disagreement. Martins (1994, pp. 123-126, 132-133, 138) treats Dâw as a pitch accent language whose one H tone per word 'functions as the accent' and says intensity stress exists only at clause level (pitch = word level, stress = clause level, the reverse of Portuguese). Simmons & Epps (2025, ms pp. 3-6) treat the same facts as fixed word-final lexical stress with an obligatory cumulative H that docks on the stressed syllable ('a word-accent system parasitic on lexical stress'), and state outright that 'Stress in Dâw is consistently word-final'; they note (ms p. 5-6) that their analysis differs from S. Martins 2004 / V. Martins 2005 in exactly this respect. Both sources put the word-level prominence (H tone) on the final syllable of polysyllables, so the catalog's final placement is supported by both; only the label (stress vs pitch accent) is contested. Obert 2019 could not be opened.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed final stress on the prosodic word, non-distinctive/demarcative, no weight, a closed listed set of extrametric suffixes, tone lexical and co-occurring with stress in simple/compound words) is taken verbatim from the dedicated stress section of the only reference grammar of Dâw (Martins 2004, LOT 98, 685 pp), which we hold as an open full-text PDF; the quotation and page/PDF locators check out exactly, and the morphology chapter of the same work restates the extrametric-suffix rule consistently. Glottolog lists no later grammar or phonology; Obert 2019 is open but its host was unreachable today; it is the one item worth downloading later for independent confirmation. no reclassification or identity issue.
